quests.instruction: Say “be honest” at normal speed. What usually connects the two vowels at the boundary?
options: The two vowels merge into one long vowel: “beeonest”
A quick /w/ sound slides between them: “bee-wonest”
A quick /j/ (a “y” sound) slides between them: “bee-yonest”
quests.correctAnswer: A quick /j/ (a “y” sound) slides between them: “bee-yonest”
quests.hint: Say “be” on its own and notice where your tongue is at the end of the vowel. Then say “honest” straight after it.
quests.explanation: “Be” ends in a high front vowel, and “honest” begins with a vowel sound because the “h” is silent. When two vowels meet, speakers often add a light /j/ glide between them, so it sounds like “bee-yonest”. This helps a listener hear two words instead of one long vowel.
quests.phoneticRule: After vowels made with the tongue high and forward, such as /iː/, a light /j/ glide is commonly heard between the vowel and a following vowel-initial word.

quests.instruction: In “say it”, which sound is heard between “say” and “it” in fast speech?
options: A /w/ glide
A /j/ glide
A /t/ that has moved back from “it”
quests.correctAnswer: A /j/ glide
quests.hint: The vowel in “say” ends with the tongue high at the front of the mouth. Which glide fits that position?
quests.explanation: “Say” ends with the vowel /eɪ/, whose last movement is towards /ɪ/. From that position the natural bridge to the next vowel is /j/, so it sounds like “say-yit”. The /t/ stays at the end of “it”; it does not move backward.
quests.phoneticRule: Diphthongs ending in /ɪ/ (such as /eɪ/, /aɪ/ and /ɔɪ/) are typically followed by a /j/ glide before a vowel-initial word.

quests.instruction: Apply the idea to “she asked” in “She asked me first.” Which spoken form fits?
options: “she-wasked”, with a /w/ glide as in “go on”
“she-yasked”, with a /j/ glide
“she-hasked”, with an /h/ inserted to keep the vowels apart
quests.correctAnswer: “she-yasked”, with a /j/ glide
quests.hint: Say “she” and hold the vowel: notice how high your tongue is. That position points to one of the glides.
quests.explanation: “She” ends in /iː/ and “asked” begins with a vowel, so a light /j/ appears between them: “she-yasked”. It is not an added letter; it is a small movement of the tongue. Hearing it stops you expecting an “h” or a pause.
quests.phoneticRule: The /j/ glide is a transitional movement rather than a full word-initial consonant, so it is usually brief and lighter than a /j/ at the start of a word.

quests.instruction: What connects “go” and “on” in a fluent “go on”?
options: A quick /w/ glide: “go-won”
A quick /j/ glide: “go-yon”
The two vowels merge into one: “goon”
quests.correctAnswer: A quick /w/ glide: “go-won”
quests.hint: Say “go” and notice how your lips end up: rounded. Then move straight into “on”.
quests.explanation: “Go” ends with /əʊ/, which finishes with rounded lips. From there the easiest bridge to a vowel is a light /w/: “go-won”. Without it, the two words could sound like a single word, “goon”.
quests.phoneticRule: Vowels that end with lip rounding (/əʊ/, /uː/, /aʊ/) are commonly followed by a /w/ glide before a vowel-initial word.

quests.instruction: Why does “do it” sound like “do-wit”?
options: The /d/ of “do” moves onto “it”, giving “doo-dit”
The /t/ of “it” moves back to “do”, giving “doo-tit”
“Do” ends in a rounded vowel, so a light /w/ bridges to “it”
quests.correctAnswer: “Do” ends in a rounded vowel, so a light /w/ bridges to “it”
quests.hint: Look at the last sound of “do”. Is it a consonant or a vowel, and what shape are your lips in?
quests.explanation: “Do” ends in the vowel /uː/, not a consonant, so there is no consonant to move onto “it”. Instead the rounded lips produce a light /w/ as you go on to “it”: “do-wit”. This is why vowel-final words follow a different linking pattern from consonant-final ones.
quests.phoneticRule: A word ending in a vowel has no final consonant to relocate; the connection to a following vowel is made by a glide instead.

quests.instruction: Apply the idea to “no idea” in “I have no idea.” Which spoken form fits?
options: “no-widea”, with a /w/ glide
“no-yidea”, with a /j/ glide
“no-didea”, with a /d/ added to separate the words
quests.correctAnswer: “no-widea”, with a /w/ glide
quests.hint: The first word ends with the same rounded-lip vowel as “go”. Which glide followed that one?
quests.explanation: “No” ends with /əʊ/ and “idea” begins with a vowel, so a light /w/ bridges them: “no-widea”. The phrase is a very common reply, and the glide is one reason it can sound like “no-wi-dea” to a beginner.
quests.phoneticRule: The glide depends on where the mouth is at the end of the first vowel, so the same rounded ending gives /w/ in “go on”, “do it” and “no idea”.

quests.instruction: Which glide fits “we all”, even though the word “we” begins with a “w”?
options: /w/, because the first word starts with a “w”
/j/, because “we” ends in a high front vowel
No glide: the vowels simply touch each other
quests.correctAnswer: /j/, because “we” ends in a high front vowel
quests.hint: Ignore how the word begins. The glide depends on the way the vowel ends.
quests.explanation: The start of “we” is irrelevant; what matters is the vowel at the end, /iː/. That vowel ends with the tongue high and forward, so a /j/ glide bridges to “all”: “wee-yall”. A /w/ would need a rounded ending like the vowel in “do”.
quests.phoneticRule: The glide is determined by the final vowel's shape (high front gives /j/, rounded gives /w/), not by the spelling or the initial consonant of the word.

quests.instruction: “We all” took a /j/ glide. Which glide does “too easy” take, and why?
options: /w/, because “too” ends in a rounded vowel
/j/, because “easy” begins with the vowel /iː/
/j/, because “too” also ends with a vowel
quests.correctAnswer: /w/, because “too” ends in a rounded vowel
quests.hint: Check the vowel that ends the first word, not the vowel that starts the second.
quests.explanation: The glide depends on the vowel before it. “Too” ends in /uː/, which is made with rounded lips, so a light /w/ follows: “too-weasy”. The start of “easy” does not decide it. Using this rule, you can predict either glide without memorising individual phrases.
quests.phoneticRule: The preceding vowel selects the glide: a rounded ending gives /w/ and a high front ending gives /j/, regardless of which vowel follows.

quests.instruction: You are told to “throw away” some old papers. Which spoken form fits the phrase?
options: “throw-yaway”, with a /j/ glide
“thro-away”, with the vowels running together and no sound between them
“throw-waway”, with a /w/ glide
quests.correctAnswer: “throw-waway”, with a /w/ glide
quests.hint: The last vowel of “throw” is the same rounded ending you heard in “go”. Predict the glide from that.
quests.explanation: “Throw” ends in /əʊ/, a rounded vowel, so a light /w/ bridges to “away”: “throw-waway”. If you meet a new word that ends in a vowel, ask how your lips and tongue finish it; that tells you which glide to expect.
quests.phoneticRule: Glide prediction is a two-step check: identify the ending vowel's shape, then choose /j/ for high front endings or /w/ for rounded endings.

quests.instruction: You tell a friend that a place is “far away”. Which spoken form fits in a General British accent?
options: “far … away”, with a small stop after “far”
“fa-away”, with the two vowels simply touching
“fa-raway”, with a linking /r/ before “away”
quests.correctAnswer: “fa-raway”, with a linking /r/ before “away”
quests.hint: The word “far” is spelled with a final “r”. In this accent that letter can be heard in only one situation. Which one?
quests.explanation: In General British English, an “r” at the end of a word is normally silent. But when a vowel follows, the /r/ is pronounced and links the two words: “fa-raway”. The spelling gives a clue about which sound may appear. Rhotic accents such as most American English pronounce the /r/ in “far” in every position.
quests.phoneticRule: In non-rhotic accents, a word-final “r” spelling is pronounced as /r/ when a vowel-initial word follows (linking /r/) but is silent before a consonant or a pause.

quests.instruction: In “four of us”, which sound is heard at the start of “of”?
options: The /f/ from the start of “four”
A linking /r/ from the end of “four”
A light /w/ that comes from the rounded vowel of “four”
quests.correctAnswer: A linking /r/ from the end of “four”
quests.hint: Compare the spelling of “four” with “go”. One of them ends in a letter that can be heard before a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Four” ends in a vowel, but it is spelled with a final “r”. In this accent that /r/ returns before a vowel, so you hear “fo-ruv-us” rather than a /w/ glide. A word like “go” has no spelled “r”, so it takes a glide instead.
quests.phoneticRule: A spelled final “r” signals a linking /r/ before a vowel; without that spelling, a vowel-final word takes a glide (/j/ or /w/) instead.

quests.instruction: Apply the pattern to “care about” in “I care about this.” Which spoken form fits?
options: “keh-rabout”, with a linking /r/ before “about”
“keh-yabout”, with a /j/ glide
“keh-wabout”, with a /w/ glide
quests.correctAnswer: “keh-rabout”, with a linking /r/ before “about”
quests.hint: Look at the last letters of “care”. They may decide which sound bridges the words.
quests.explanation: “Care” ends in a spelled “re”, so a linking /r/ appears before “about”: “keh-rabout”. Because the vowel in “care” is a diphthong, some learners expect a glide, but the spelling is the better clue.
quests.phoneticRule: The linking /r/ appears after vowels that are spelled with a final “r” or “re”, including centring diphthongs such as those in “care”, “here” and “sure”.

quests.instruction: Predict which sound joins “there” and “is” in “There is a problem.”
options: A linking /r/: “theh-riz”
A /j/ glide: “theh-yiz”
Nothing: the two vowels simply touch
quests.correctAnswer: A linking /r/: “theh-riz”
quests.hint: Predict first, then look at the spelling of “there”. Its last letters are the clue.
quests.explanation: “There” ends in a spelled “re”, and “is” begins with a vowel, so the /r/ is heard: “theh-riz”. Statements with “there is” or “there are” are extremely common, so this link is worth expecting.
quests.phoneticRule: Existential “there” is followed by a linking /r/ before a vowel-initial verb, as in “there is”, “there are” and “there isn’t”.

quests.instruction: Choose the explanation that fits “after all” in a fluent phrase like “It worked out after all.”
options: The /t/ moves onto “all”: “af-tall”
The word “all” is reduced so far that it merges with “after”
The final “r” of “after” is pronounced because “all” starts with a vowel: “af-te-rawl”
quests.correctAnswer: The final “r” of “after” is pronounced because “all” starts with a vowel: “af-te-rawl”
quests.hint: The word “after” ends in a spelled “r”. Compare with what follows it: a vowel or a consonant?
quests.explanation: Before a consonant or a pause, the “r” in “after” is silent in this accent. Before “all”, a vowel-initial word, it returns as a linking /r/: “af-te-rawl”. The /t/ stays where it is, in the middle of “after”.
quests.phoneticRule: A linking /r/ connects a word-final “r” to a following vowel; sounds inside the word, such as the /t/ in “after”, do not move.

quests.instruction: Apply the pattern to “for example” at the start of an explanation. Which spoken form fits?
options: “for … example”, with a small stop after “for”
“fuh-rexample”, with the /r/ starting “example”
“fuh-wexample”, with a /w/ glide
quests.correctAnswer: “fuh-rexample”, with the /r/ starting “example”
quests.hint: Say the phrase as you would when introducing an illustration. What happens to the last letter of “for”?
quests.explanation: “For” ends in a spelled “r”, so before “example” the /r/ is pronounced: “fuh-rexample”. The word often has a weak vowel in fast speech, but the linking /r/ is unaffected. Hearing it helps you spot “for” at the start of clauses.
quests.phoneticRule: The linking /r/ works with weak forms as well as strong forms of function words such as “for”, “or” and “are”.

quests.instruction: Speakers of General British and General American may say “car park” differently. What is the difference?
options: General American keeps the /r/ in “car”, while General British usually drops it before a consonant
British speakers add an /r/ and American speakers drop it
Both accents drop the /r/ because “park” starts with a consonant
quests.correctAnswer: British speakers add an /r/ and American speakers drop it
quests.hint: Think about what the letter “r” does in each accent before a consonant.
quests.explanation: General American is rhotic: the /r/ in “car” is pronounced everywhere. General British is non-rhotic: the /r/ is heard only before a vowel, so before “park” it is dropped. Both are normal; the linking /r/ you learned is where the two accents overlap.
quests.phoneticRule: In rhotic accents the /r/ is pronounced whenever it is spelled; in non-rhotic accents it is pronounced only before a vowel, so the accents agree before vowels and differ before consonants and pauses.

quests.instruction: Which statement about the /r/ in “clear up” is true for both General British and General American speakers?
options: Both pronounce the /r/, because a vowel follows
Neither pronounces it, because “clear” ends in a vowel sound
Only General American speakers pronounce it, because that accent is rhotic
quests.correctAnswer: Both pronounce the /r/, because a vowel follows
quests.hint: Test the phrase against both rules: the rhotic rule and the non-rhotic rule. What do they say about a following vowel?
quests.explanation: Before a vowel, both accents pronounce the /r/: General American because it does so in every position, and General British as a linking /r/. So “clear up” is heard as “clea-rup” in both. The accents differ mainly before consonants and at the end of an utterance.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking /r/ is the common ground between rhotic and non-rhotic accents: before a vowel-initial word the /r/ is present in both.

quests.instruction: In “over there at ten”, which /r/ do General British speakers pronounce?
options: The one at the end of “there”, because “at” begins with a vowel
The one at the end of “over”, because “there” follows it
Both, because both words are spelled with “r”
quests.correctAnswer: The one at the end of “there”, because “at” begins with a vowel
quests.hint: Check the sound that follows each word ending in “r”, and see which one is followed by a vowel.
quests.explanation: Only “there” is followed by a vowel-initial word (“at”), so its /r/ is pronounced: “o-vuh theh-rat ten”. “Over” is followed by “there”, which begins with a consonant, so its /r/ stays silent. The spelling alone does not decide; the next sound does.
quests.phoneticRule: In a non-rhotic accent the pronunciation of a final /r/ depends on the following sound, so the same spelling can be silent in one position and pronounced in another.

quests.instruction: Someone knocks and you call out “Who is it?” Which spoken form fits the start of the question?
options: “who … is”, with a small stop between the words
“who-yiz”, with a /j/ glide
“who-wiz”, with a /w/ glide
quests.correctAnswer: “who-wiz”, with a /w/ glide
quests.hint: Say “who” and hold the vowel: the lips are rounded. Which glide follows from that shape?
quests.explanation: “Who” ends in /uː/, so a light /w/ bridges to “is”: “who-wiz”. Doorstep and phone questions are short and quick, so this glide is part of how they flow.
quests.phoneticRule: Wh-question words that end in a rounded vowel, such as “who” and “how”, take a /w/ glide before a vowel-initial verb.

quests.instruction: Choose the spoken form that fits “why is it” in “Why is it so late?”
options: “why-wiz it”, with a /w/ glide
“why … iz it”, with no link at all
“why-yi-zit”, with a /j/ glide and then the /z/ joining “it”
quests.correctAnswer: “why-yi-zit”, with a /j/ glide and then the /z/ joining “it”
quests.hint: This phrase has two boundaries with different links. Handle them one at a time.
quests.explanation: “Why” ends in /aɪ/, so a light /j/ bridges to “is”. Then “is” ends in /z/ and “it” begins with a vowel, so the /z/ moves onto “it”: “why-yi-zit”. Two different kinds of link can sit side by side in a short question.
quests.phoneticRule: A question can combine a glide link (after a vowel-final word) and a consonant link (after a consonant-final word).

quests.instruction: Apply what you know to “where is it” in “Where is it now?” Which spoken form fits?
options: “weh-yiz it”, with a /j/ glide
“weh-ri-zit”, with a linking /r/ and then the /z/ joining “it”
“weh-wiz it”, with a /w/ glide
quests.correctAnswer: “weh-ri-zit”, with a linking /r/ and then the /z/ joining “it”
quests.hint: The question word ends in letters that can be heard before a vowel. Which sound do they suggest?
quests.explanation: “Where” ends in a spelled “re”, so before “is” a linking /r/ is heard: “weh-riz”. The /z/ of “is” then joins “it”. So this question uses a linking /r/ rather than a glide, and the deciding clue is the spelling.
quests.phoneticRule: Question words spelled with a final “r” or “re” (where, there, here) take a linking /r/, whereas those without it (who, why, how) take a glide.

quests.instruction: Which two links happen in “try it on”?
options: A /j/ glide after “try”, then the /t/ of “it” joining “on”
A /w/ glide after “try”, then the /t/ of “it” joining “on”
A linking /r/ after “try”, then a /j/ glide after “it”
quests.correctAnswer: A /j/ glide after “try”, then the /t/ of “it” joining “on”
quests.hint: Split the phrase into its two boundaries and decide separately what kind of sound comes before each vowel.
quests.explanation: “Try” ends in /aɪ/, so a light /j/ bridges to “it”. “It” ends in the consonant /t/, so the /t/ moves onto “on”: “try-yi-ton”. Vowel-final and consonant-final words behave differently, and phrases often contain both.
quests.phoneticRule: Each boundary chooses its own link: vowel-final words use a glide (or /r/ when spelled with “r”), while consonant-final words hand their final consonant to the next vowel.

quests.instruction: Which boundary in “be out early” is bridged by a glide rather than by a moved consonant?
options: Between “out” and “early”
Between “be” and “out”
Both boundaries
quests.correctAnswer: Between “be” and “out”
quests.hint: Sort the boundaries by what the first word ends in: a vowel or a consonant.
quests.explanation: The /t/ at the end of “out” moves onto “early”, which is a consonant link. The boundary after “be” is different: “be” ends in a vowel, so a /j/ glide appears instead. The full chunk is “bee-yow-tur-lee”.
quests.phoneticRule: In a chain of links, vowel-final words contribute a glide and consonant-final words contribute their last consonant.

quests.instruction: Someone admits, “I owe it.” Which spoken form fits the two boundaries in “I owe it”?
options: “I-wo-yit”, with the two glides in the wrong order
“I-yo-it”, with a glide after “I” only, and “owe” and “it” touching
“I-yo-wit”, with /j/ after “I” and /w/ after “owe”
quests.correctAnswer: “I-yo-wit”, with /j/ after “I” and /w/ after “owe”
quests.hint: Both “I” and “owe” end in vowels. Work out each glide from the shape of the vowel it ends with.
quests.explanation: “I” ends in /aɪ/, so a /j/ bridges to “owe”. “Owe” ends in /əʊ/, so a /w/ bridges to “it”: “I-yo-wit”. Two glides in a row are common in short phrases and can make them hard to segment.
quests.phoneticRule: Adjacent vowel-final words each supply their own glide, so different glides can occur in sequence within one short chunk.

quests.instruction: A teacher says “to us” slowly, with a slight break between the words. Another says it quickly with a glide. Which statement is fair?
options: The slow version is an error, because vowel-initial words have to be linked
Both are normal: a break is common in careful speech, and a glide is common in fluent speech
The fast version is an error, because a glide adds a sound that is not in the word
quests.correctAnswer: Both are normal: a break is common in careful speech, and a glide is common in fluent speech
quests.hint: Think about the difference between speaking for clarity and speaking at conversation speed.
quests.explanation: Linking and glide insertion are typical of fluent speech. In careful or emphatic speech, speakers may separate the words, sometimes with a tiny closure of the throat before the vowel. Both are normal; the choice depends on speed and emphasis. For listening, what matters is recognising either version.
quests.phoneticRule: Glide insertion and a short break (hiatus) are both normal realisations of a vowel + vowel boundary; the choice varies with speech rate, emphasis and style.

quests.instruction: In a meeting you say “I agree” with a slight pause after “I” for emphasis. What is that pause doing?
options: It shows that you have forgotten the glide
It turns the phrase into two unrelated sentences
It separates the words for emphasis, which is normal and does not change the meaning
quests.correctAnswer: It separates the words for emphasis, which is normal and does not change the meaning
quests.hint: Consider why a speaker might slow down and separate two words on purpose.
quests.explanation: A break between two vowels is a way to give one word extra prominence, such as the pronoun in “I agree”. It is a natural variation, and it does not change the words. At everyday speed, the same phrase would probably have a light glide: “I-yagree”.
quests.phoneticRule: Separating vowel-initial words with a small break is a normal way to add emphasis; linking is the usual pattern at conversational speed, not a rule that must be followed.

quests.instruction: Which delivery of “the end” fits a relaxed conversation?
options: “thee-yend”, with a light glide between the words
“the … end”, with a firm stop of air before “end” each time
“thee end”, with the two vowels held apart for a full beat
quests.correctAnswer: “thee-yend”, with a light glide between the words
quests.hint: Choose the version you would use when chatting with a friend, not when dictating.
quests.explanation: In relaxed speech the words run together and a light glide fills the gap: “thee-yend”. Firm breaks and held-apart vowels are useful for dictation or emphasis, but they sound stiff in conversation. So the fluent version is the better model for everyday talk.
quests.phoneticRule: For everyday conversation the linked or glided version is the natural default; separated delivery is a marked style used for clarity or emphasis.

quests.instruction: Which kind of link is heard in “here in town”?
options: A light /j/ glide between the vowels
A linking /r/
A consonant that has moved back from “town”
quests.correctAnswer: A linking /r/
quests.hint: Check how “here” ends, both in spelling and in sound.
quests.explanation: “Here” ends in a spelled “re”, so before the vowel of “in” a linking /r/ is heard: “hee-rin town”. It is not a glide, because the /r/ comes from the spelling, and it is not a consonant moved from the next word.
quests.phoneticRule: Identify the link type by asking two questions: does the first word end in a consonant sound, and if it ends in a vowel, does its spelling include a final “r”?

quests.instruction: Which link is heard between “to” and “eat” in a fluent “to eat”?
options: A light /w/ glide that bridges the two vowels
A light /j/ glide that bridges the two vowels
A linking /r/ that appears before “eat”
quests.correctAnswer: A light /w/ glide that bridges the two vowels
quests.hint: Look at how your lips end the vowel in “to”.
quests.explanation: “To” ends in a rounded vowel, so a light /w/ bridges to “eat”: “too-weat”. It is the same pattern as “go on” and “do it”.
quests.phoneticRule: The link type follows the final sound of the first word: a rounded vowel gives /w/, a high front vowel gives /j/, a vowel with a spelled “r” gives /r/, and a consonant moves onto the next word.

quests.instruction: Your teacher says, “Go over it again.” Which pair of links matches “go over it”?
options: A /j/ glide, then a consonant moved from “it”
A linking /r/, then a /w/ glide
A /w/ glide, then a linking /r/
quests.correctAnswer: A /w/ glide, then a linking /r/
quests.hint: Take the two boundaries in order: what does “go” end in, and what does “over” end in?
quests.explanation: “Go” ends in /əʊ/, so a /w/ glide bridges to “over”. “Over” is spelled with a final “r”, so before “it” a linking /r/ is heard: “go-wo-vuh-rit”. One phrase can therefore use two different bridges.
quests.phoneticRule: A single phrase can combine a glide and a linking /r/; each boundary is decided separately by the ending of the word before it.
